answer_text:
Let

\[
X_t=\mu t+\sigma B_t.
\]

Since the exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing,

\[
\liminf_{t\to\infty} e^{X_t}
=
\exp\!\left(\liminf_{t\to\infty} X_t\right).
\]

Thus the event

\[
\left\{\liminf_{t\to\infty} e^{\mu t+\sigma B_t}>1\right\}
\]

is equivalent to

\[
\left\{\liminf_{t\to\infty} (\mu t+\sigma B_t)>0\right\}.
\]

Now use the standard fact for Brownian motion that

\[
\frac{B_t}{t}\to 0 \qquad \text{a.s. as } t\to\infty.
\]

Therefore, since \(\mu>0\),

\[
\frac{\mu t+\sigma B_t}{t}
=
\mu+\sigma\frac{B_t}{t}
\to \mu>0
\qquad \text{a.s.}
\]

Hence there exists a random time \(T\) such that for all \(t\ge T\),

\[
\mu t+\sigma B_t \ge \frac{\mu}{2}t.
\]

Consequently,

\[
e^{\mu t+\sigma B_t}\ge e^{\frac{\mu}{2}t}\to\infty
\qquad \text{a.s.}
\]

So

\[
\liminf_{t\to\infty} e^{\mu t+\sigma B_t}=\infty>1
\qquad \text{a.s.}
\]

Thus the probability of the stated event is

\[
\boxed{1}
\]
